Hong Kong Monetary Authority Last week, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority announced the introduction of the “ART” Framework to support responsible adoption of AI in the banking sector. Initiatives under the “ART” Framework include: -- An AI training data sharing platform in collaboration with Hong Kong Cyberport Management Company Limited (Cyberport) and the University of Hong Kong, with data quality assurance as a core design principle; and -- Further testing of agentic AI applications through the GenAI Sandbox++2 and an upcoming discussion paper on a proposed supervisory framework for agentic AI governance, exploring intent-anchored accountability, a registry of material AI agents, and effective intervention mechanisms. “The progression from generative to agentic AI represents an important new stage of innovation for the banking sector,” Arthur Yuen, deputy chief executive of the HKMA, said. Asia’s financial centres are competing in areas of AI innovation as much as on other lines. A sign of the sensitivities came in a report entitled The Standard (of Hong Kong), on 6 October, saying that the HKMA has questioned HSBC’s decision to set up a Global AI Centre of Excellence in Singapore instead of Hong Kong. The HKMA has also discussed with HSBC and Standard Chartered about reallocating more managerial and senior positions to mainland China, the publication said. The report said HKMA has declined to comment on such speculation.

title: Huntington Bank rolls out new Google AI platform to assist small businesses
excerpt: § Filed Dispatch Broadsheet Edition. Huntington Bank rolls out new Google AI platform to assist small businesses. By Dave Kovaleski Financial Regulation News 21 hours ago. 💬 0. The Huntington National Bank introduced a new AI-powered operating system built with Google Cloud’s Gemini AI platform. © Shutterstock The system, called the 1866 Studio , was named for the year Huntington was founded. The 1866 Studio honors the bank’s legacy of empowering businesses by bringing together guidance, financial intelligence, digital tools and human expertise into a single, connected experience for small business owners. The 1866 Studio is designed to simplify the often complex and time-consuming demands of starting and running a business. “We are continually looking for new ways to help business owners navigate challenges, seize opportunities and spend more time focused on the financial success and growth of their businesses. The 1866 Studio is the next evolution of that commitment, bringing together Huntington’s expertise and Gemini platform to help owners make more informed decisions and spend more time building the businesses they imagined,” Brant Standridge, president of Huntington Bank, said. The 1866 Studio will leverage Huntington’s small business and financial expertise along with an AI-powered experience built using Google’s platform to build, scale, govern and optimize agents. Combined with Google’s Gemini models, the platform allows Huntington to offer business owners an intelligent, connected operating system that helps them navigate decisions with greater confidence and efficiency. “The future of small business banking is about delivering expertise and guidance in the moments customers need it most,” Rohit Bhat, general manager and managing director, Financial Services, Google Cloud, said. “By using Gemini platform and Gemini frontier models to build The 1866 Studio, Huntington is creating an innovative experience that helps small business owners move from information to action. ”. Initial AI capabilities, including agentic workflows, equip entrepreneurs to turn business ideas into actionable plans, navigate startup requirements, strengthen their brand, identify funding sources, enable funding readiness and plan for growth. Specifically, the platform can help with:. Business launch support: With built-in AI agents, owners can navigate the steps required to start a business, from entity selection and registration to licensing and operational setup, while generating a customized action plan to help move from idea to launch. Marketing and campaign creation: Leveraging multimodal Gemini models, owners can instantly generate tailored marketing collateral, digital ad copy and social media campaigns. Loan readiness assistance: AI-powered agents help owners evaluate financing readiness by identifying potential gaps, explaining lender expectations and recommending actions that can strengthen eligibility for future financing opportunities. “Agentic AI workflows that help carry out tasks are one part of this end-to-end operating system,” Vijay Konduru, head of innovation and AI products at Huntington, said. “Alongside them are relevant, personalized expert content and an AI assistant that helps owners both monitor their business operations and finances and manage and orchestrate daily work. ”. The 1866 Studio builds on Huntington’s multi-year strategic partnership with Google Cloud to modernize technology, advance AI capabilities and accelerate innovation. Interested small business owners and entrepreneurs, not limited to Huntington customers, can sign up now for early access to the 1866 Studio. title: Banks must prepare for AI failures before customers pay the price, UK watchdog warns
excerpt: . Industry News Finance. 4 min read. Banks must prepare for AI failures before customers pay the price, UK watchdog warns. Filip TRUȚĂ. October 21, 2026. Britain’s financial regulator is warning financial institutions that increasingly autonomous AI systems could cause widespread disruption, expose customers to cyber threats, and make accountability harder to establish. It wants firms to report serious AI failures and near-misses before they turn into bigger problems. Artificial intelligence is rapidly becoming part of everyday banking, from customer service chatbots to fraud detection and automated financial decisions. But what happens when an AI system makes a costly mistake, exposes sensitive information, or nearly triggers a disaster?. The UK's Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) wants financial firms to prepare for precisely those scenarios — and report significant AI-related failures, including incidents that were narrowly avoided. Key points. The FCA wants financial institutions to report significant AI failures and near-misses, not just incidents that cause actual damage. 86% of financial firms now use AI, the regulator says, citing an upcoming joint survey with the Bank of England. Autonomous AI agents could introduce new cybersecurity risks as they gain the ability to manage payments, investments and other transactions. Firms are being urged to stress-test AI systems, maintain human oversight and prepare fallback procedures. Consumers are increasingly using general-purpose AI chatbots for financial advice, often without understanding the limits of their protections. AI failures could become a regulatory priority. Jessica Rusu, the FCA's chief data, information and intelligence officer, warned that the financial sector's growing dependence on AI creates risks that existing safeguards must address. "Poorly governed AI can create consumer harm, cyber vulnerabilities and operational failures, potentially at much greater speed and scale," Rusu said at Bloomberg's UK Policy Series on Oct. 19. The regulator already requires firms to report major operational incidents. Rusu argued that this obligation must also cover significant AI failures and near-misses. A near-miss might involve an AI system attempting an unauthorized transaction that is blocked by a security control, or a chatbot generating dangerously incorrect financial information that’s spotted before reaching customers. Neither scenario necessarily inflicts immediate harm, but both could reveal weaknesses that might cause serious problems later. The idea is similar to safety reporting in aviation, where investigating narrowly avoided accidents can help prevent future disasters. The FCA's announcement signals a supervisory expectation, rather than a new, finalized AI-specific reporting regime. When AI starts making financial decisions. The FCA is particularly concerned about the emergence of agentic AI — systems capable of taking actions on behalf of users rather than simply answering questions. Unlike conventional chatbots, AI agents could compare financial products, initiate payments, manage investments and interact with other automated systems. Such capabilities promise greater convenience but also introduce new security challenges. An AI assistant that merely provides inaccurate information can mislead a customer. An autonomous agent acting on that information could potentially execute an unwanted transaction before anyone notices. Compromised AI agents, manipulated instructions, excessive permissions and weak authentication could also create opportunities for cybercriminals. For example, an attacker might try to manipulate an AI-powered financial assistant into changing payment details or disclosing sensitive customer information. The regulator wants the industry to develop clearer safeguards around agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and transaction execution. excerpt: An article from. FDIC’s Hill mulls agentic AI deposit impact. Travis Hill, speaking Tuesday in Las Vegas, also said he sees potential for AI to help the banking agency become more efficient in aspects of supervision and failed bank resolution. Published Oct. 21, 2026. Caitlin Mullen Senior Editor. Share Copy link. Email. LinkedIn. X/Twitter. Facebook. Print. License. Add us on Google. LAS VEGAS – A top banking regulator couldn’t escape one of the biggest artificial intelligence-related questions in the banking world over the past week. AI agents moving deposits on behalf of customers is “the big thing that we're thinking about,” and “that a lot of the banks are thinking about,” Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. Chair Travis Hill said Tuesday at an Axios event on governing the agentic economy in Las Vegas. “There's just a big question of, to what extent are depositors going to delegate that type of decision-making authority to these types of agents?” Hill said. “There certainly will be some,” he said. “The question is, how many and how big of an impact is that going to have on the overall landscape?”. The launch of Meta’s AI assistant Muse and the addition of Stripe’s Link wallet to enable Muse to transact on behalf of consumers have reignited conversation around agentic AI cash sorting concerns for lenders and the threat such activity could pose to their deposit businesses. Big banks have pointed to safety and soundness concerns related to AI agents’ access. Citi and Bank of America have joined JPMorgan Chase in blocking customers’ external AI agents from accessing customer bank accounts. JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said consumers need to understand the risks of using AI agents, because “there’s a liability transfer. ”. Other bank executives, such as PNC CEO Bill Demchak – who spoke Monday at the Money20/20 conference – and Fifth Third CFO Bryan Preston have indicated accountability questions need to be settled before agents carry out transactions on behalf of their customers. Hill on Tuesday also pointed to “a long-standing progression” over decades of simpler money movement, particularly if customers are interested in maximizing the rate they receive on deposits. Still, many bank customers earn close to zero interest. “Oftentimes, it's that depositors value other things,” he said. About half of deposits in the system are corporate, Hill said. “A manufacturing company might have sophisticated needs that a bank is providing that justify why they're earning a small return on the deposit account,” he said. At the Axios event, Hill was also asked why revised model risk management guidance issued by the FDIC, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Reserve earlier this year didn’t address generative and agentic AI. The FDIC chair said the guidance both in its prior form and current form doesn’t “work well for agentic AI and generative AI, which is a very rapidly evolving technology. ”. “We are continuing to think about future guidance in that area,” Hill said. “We are considering soliciting information from the public about how we should think about it from a supervisory standpoint. ”. Regulators are trying to make sure they’re staying current as the technology changes, while being thoughtful and deliberative, he said. Much like industry players, the FDIC is adopting AI in the pursuit of efficiency, although Hill said he would like to see the agency move a bit faster. “We do have a couple of tools that we're using right now,” Hill said during an earlier appearance Tuesday, at the Money20/20 conference in Las Vegas. “We are trying to be, I'd say, more strategic in how we build out those tools, to ensure that we're making progress and going to achieve some of our longer-term goals in a reasonable amount of time. ”. Hill said he sees potential for AI to help the FDIC in some aspects of supervision and failed bank resolution. Economy & Business. Devdiscourse News Desk | Seoul | Korea Rep. Updated: 21-10-2026 16:52 IST | Created: 21-10-2026 16:52 IST. Image Credit: ChatGPT. The World Bank Group has launched its first digital strategy to help developing countries make internet access more affordable, improve public services and create jobs, bringing its public and private sector capabilities together around countries’ needs. The strategy connects four priorities: reliable connectivity, cheaper devices and data, stronger digital services and skills, and the foundations needed to use artificial intelligence. Internet use reached just 23 per cent in low-income countries, compared with 94 per cent in high-income countries, revealing a divide that extends beyond the availability of networks. Many people already live within coverage areas but cannot afford smartphones or data. Others lack digital skills or access to services that meet their needs, leaving them disconnected from opportunities even when a signal is available. The World Bank Group plans to help countries address gaps throughout their networks, from international cables and national connections to the infrastructure serving homes, businesses, schools and clinics. Shared infrastructure, greater competition, public financing and guarantees form part of its approach to attracting private investment into underserved markets. In places without reliable electricity or connectivity, the strategy supports planning both together. Affordability will receive separate attention through efforts to reduce the cost of entry-level smartphones and broadband services. Partnerships with manufacturers, mobile operators, financial institutions and refurbishment businesses could help bring prices down and expand responsible payment options that let customers spread costs over time. Connecting digital services and skills to the jobs challenge. The strategy arrives as developing countries face constrained resources and growing pressure to provide employment. Over the next 10 to 15 years, around 1. 2 billion young people will reach working age in these countries, but their economies are projected to create about 420 million jobs. World Bank Group President Ajay Banga said digital technology can help countries create employment and stretch limited resources, provided that reliable connections, affordable devices, useful services and digital skills develop together. Technology can support activity across the institution’s five priority sectors: infrastructure and energy, agribusiness, health care, tourism and value-added manufacturing. For businesses, that could mean reaching more customers, improving productivity and accessing finance; for governments, it could reduce the cost of delivering public services. The strategy includes support for dependable digital identification, payment systems and secure information-sharing, making public and private services easier to access. Digital literacy and training linked to employment will help people and small businesses use those systems safely and productively. Privacy, cybersecurity and protection against fraud run across all four priorities. Making practical AI tools accessible to more countries. title: HSBC’s AI-Driven Restructuring: Transformation and Displacement in UK Wealth Management

Sweeping Job Cuts Announced Up to 70% of Adviser Roles at Risk "Generative AI Will Destroy Certain Jobs" Shift to Digital-First Services Consultation Underway. By Mark Lim Published about 21 hours ago • 3 min read. HSBC is advancing one of the most significant workforce transformations in the global banking sector, with plans to restructure its UK wealth management division through sweeping job reductions driven directly by the accelerated adoption of artificial intelligence. The Financial Times reported yesterday that the bank intends to cut roughly half of all management and specialist roles, while financial adviser positions could drop by as much as 70% — changes that will reshape how wealth advice is delivered and underscore the reality that AI is not merely augmenting work, but replacing it. The Scale of the Restructuring. The numbers are striking. While HSBC does not disclose exact headcount figures for its UK wealth business, the division employs hundreds of relationship managers, advisers, and support staff across the country. Under the proposed plan:. Approximately 50% of management and specialist positions are set to be eliminated. Up to 70% of financial adviser roles may be removed. Affected employees are expected to depart by the end of October, following ongoing internal consultations. The consultation process is already underway. HSBC has not issued detailed breakdowns by region or seniority, nor has it confirmed whether any new roles will be created to replace those lost. A request for comment from Reuters outside business hours did not receive an immediate response. In a statement provided to the Financial Times , the bank framed the changes as evolution: “We’re continuing to evolve to deliver more digitally enabled products and journeys to support our best-in-class wealth service and meet the changing needs of our customers. ”. AI as Strategy, Not Just a Tool. The restructuring is not a cost-cutting measure disguised as modernisation — it is the direct execution of a leadership vision that has been stated openly and repeatedly. Since becoming group chief executive in 2024, Georges Elhedery has positioned generative AI at the absolute centre of HSBC’s future. Speaking at the bank’s investor day in May 2026, he was unflinching: “Generative AI will destroy certain jobs. ” Rather than softening the language, he urged employees to embrace change rather than resist it, framing displacement as inevitable and resistance as futile. Under the new operating model, AI systems will take over routine client communications, portfolio monitoring, performance reporting, risk assessment, and administrative workflow tasks that have historically occupied the majority of an adviser’s working week. The bank’s logic is that technology will handle volume, consistency, and speed, freeing the remaining workforce to focus on complex, high-value, emotionally sensitive situations intergenerational wealth transfer, business succession, major life transitions, where nuance and trust remain irreplaceable. Critics, however, question whether there will be enough of these complex cases to sustain a fraction of the current workforce. A Shift in What Wealth Management Means. For decades, wealth management has been built on relationships: knowing the client, understanding their family, their fears, their aspirations. That model is being dismantled. The emerging HSBC approach mirrors moves already underway across the industry, from private banks to retail platforms where the standard client journey becomes digital-first, AI-guided, and human-supported only at intervals. The benefits cited are efficiency, lower costs, and greater accessibility clients will be able to get answers, updates, and recommendations instantly, without waiting for an appointment. Entscheidend ist, wie Banken Breite, Tiefe und kontrollierte Delegation verbinden. Wenn wir über Künstliche Intelligenz im Banking sprechen, fehlt es nicht an Einsatzbereichen. KI unterstützt die Wissensarbeit, analysiert Daten, erkennt Muster oder strukturiert Dokumente. 92 Prozent der Banken in der EU setzen laut Europäischer Bankenaufsichtsbehörde inzwischen KI ein – vom klassischen Machine Learning bis zu generativen Anwendungen. Girokonto wählen. Partner des Bank Blogs. Die Frage ist deshalb nicht mehr, ob KI im Banking einen Platz hat. Interessanter ist, welche Form des Einsatzes zu welcher Aufgabe passt – und wie aus vielen Anwendungen eine strategische Fähigkeit der Bank entsteht. Meine These lautet: Der Wert von KI liegt nicht in spektakulären Use Cases. Er entsteht in ihrem Zusammenspiel. Digitale Agenten können viele Mitarbeiter bei ihrer täglichen Arbeit unterstützen – umso mehr, je besser die Agenten auf spezifische Aufgaben zugeschnitten sind. Perspektivisch werden solche Agenten aber nicht nur Ergebnisse liefern, sondern definierte Arbeitspakete selbstständig erledigen. KI in der Breite verändert die Wissensarbeit. Der sichtbarste Einsatzbereich generativer KI ist derzeit die tägliche Wissensarbeit. Bei uns in der LBBW steht dafür unter anderem blue. gpt zur Verfügung. Der digitale Assistent hilft, Informationen zu erschließen, Dokumente zu strukturieren oder erste Textentwürfe zu erstellen. Wir haben blue. gpt 2024 als eigene generative KI-Lösung für unsere Mitarbeiter eingeführt. Je nach Anwendungsfall greift der Chatbot auf öffentlich verfügbare Informationen oder unser Intranet zu. Der Zeitgewinn bei einer einzelnen Zusammenfassung, einer Recherche oder einer Textbearbeitung mag überschaubar wirken. In der Summe aller Anwendungen entsteht jedoch ein relevanter Effekt. Zugleich unterstützt blue. gpt darin, Aufgaben präziser zu formulieren, den notwendigen Kontext mitzugeben und Ergebnisse kritisch zu prüfen. Mit individualisierten Rollenprofilen, sogenannten Personas, entsteht ein Assistent für wiederkehrende Aufgaben. Eine Persona kann eine vorab definierte Perspektive auf ein Dokument oder einen Prozess einnehmen, Inhalte verarbeiten und Ergebnisse in einer vorgegebenen Struktur aufbereiten. Aus einer guten Idee wird so eine wiederkehrende Arbeitsweise. Eine Einsatzmöglichkeit für eine Persona ist die Vorbereitung von fachlichen Briefings. Dafür werden in dem Rollenprofil alle Wissensquellen und die Ergebnisform einmal hinterlegt. Mitarbeiter stellen die konkrete Frage an die Persona, prüfen die verwendeten Quellen und das Ergebnis. Die KI übernimmt vor allem Such-, Strukturierungs- und Vorbereitungsarbeit. KI verstehen. KI in der Breite ist deshalb kein Vorstadium der „eigentlichen“ KI. Sie ist ein eigenständiger Einsatzbereich: Viele kleine Entlastungen summieren sich, Wissen wird leichter zugänglich und Mitarbeiter entwickeln ein praktisches Verständnis dafür, welche Aufgaben sich sinnvoll delegieren lassen. Spezialisierte KI-Produkte schaffen gezielte Tiefe. Manchmal reichen allgemeine KI-Systeme nicht aus. Wenn hohe Fallzahlen, fachspezifische Regeln oder eine enge Einbindung in Abläufe erforderlich sind, braucht es spezialisierte Produkte. Solche Anwendungen können Informationen klassifizieren, Auffälligkeiten erkennen, Analysen vorbereiten oder Bearbeitungsschritte unterstützen. Bei der LBBW sind KI-basierte Werkzeuge bereits in unterschiedlichen Bereichen gezielt im Einsatz, etwa für intelligente Marktanalysen. Die Wirkungslogik ist hier eine andere als bei einem allgemeinen KI-Assistenten. Es geht um die gezielte Verbesserung eines klar beschriebenen Arbeitsabschnitts in einer spezifischen Umgebung. title: Energy regulator expands Hong Kong pact to cover AI, digital grids

News , Technology. October 13, 2026. The agreement covers renewable energy and low-carbon technologies. Singapore’s Energy Market Authority (EMA) and Hong Kong’s Electrical and Mechanical Services Department (EMSD) will continue to strengthen energy security and resilience, including artificial intelligence (AI) and digital power grids. The agencies signed a renewed memorandum of understanding to expand cooperation and the sharing of regulatory practices in electricity and gas systems and markets, renewable energy, energy efficiency and conservation, district cooling, AI, and energy integration. It will also cover low-carbon technologies such as hydrogen and carbon capture, utilisation and storage. Both agencies will collaborate through multilateral platforms, including the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, Singapore International Energy Week (SIEW), and EMSD Symposium. The agreement will facilitate knowledge sharing, technical cooperation, training and exchange programmes. It builds on a partnership between the EMA and EMSD established in 2020. “Our exchanges have provided valuable opportunities to learn from each other’s experience in areas such as electricity and gas systems, innovation and low-carbon technologies,” said EMA Chief Executive Puah Kok Keong. “We look forward to deepening our exchanges in emerging areas such as AI and digital grids and strengthening our cooperation through platforms such as SIEW,” Puah added. title: World Bank Launches AI Computing Initiative for Emerging Economies
excerpt: . SHARE. The World Bank Group has launched a new initiative to expand access to artificial intelligence infrastructure in Africa and Latin America. The programme will allow governments to use shared computing resources through a pay-as-you-go system, reducing the need to build expensive AI data centres independently. Contents. What Is the New AI Initiative? How Will the Shared AI System Work? How Will Countries Receive Financial Support? Why Is Africa a Major Focus? What Challenges Could Affect the Programme? The420 Insight: Why Does Shared AI Infrastructure Matter?. FCRF’s Chief AI Officer Certification Returns on November 14 to Prepare Future AI Leaders. What Is the New AI Initiative?. The AI Infrastructure and Readiness Initiative forms part of the World Bank Group’s first digital strategy. It aims to help emerging economies access the computing power required to develop and operate artificial intelligence systems. Cassava Technologies and NVIDIA are participating as knowledge partners. The programme focuses on making AI infrastructure more accessible to countries that face financial and technical difficulties in developing their own computing facilities. Rather than requiring every country to establish a separate data centre, the initiative promotes shared infrastructure that governments can access according to their requirements. How Will the Shared AI System Work?. The programme will provide access to graphics processing units (GPUs), which supply the computing power needed for many artificial intelligence applications. Governments will be able to use these resources through a pay-as-you-go arrangement, allowing them to access computing capacity without necessarily investing in large standalone facilities. The World Bank Group will support participating countries in assessing their computing requirements and identifying suitable infrastructure. The available options include cloud-based AI computing, distributed computing systems, regionally shared infrastructure and sovereign national computing facilities. How Will Countries Receive Financial Support?. The World Bank Group plans to establish a Digital Access Fund to support investment in digital infrastructure. The fund, anchored by the International Finance Corporation, will seek to attract capital from development institutions and private investors. This financing approach is intended to expand investment opportunities in markets where building AI infrastructure can be particularly difficult. By combining shared computing arrangements with additional financing options, the initiative seeks to reduce barriers to AI adoption in emerging economies. Why Is Africa a Major Focus?. Demand for AI computing infrastructure in Africa is expected to increase considerably over the coming years. A November 2025 projection estimated that data centre demand across the continent could rise from approximately 400 megawatts to between 1. 5 and 2. 2 gigawatts by 2030. However, the pace of expansion will depend on reliable electricity supplies, regulatory conditions and infrastructure readiness. Several AI data centre projects on the continent have faced difficulties. One project in Kenya was reported to have stalled because of substantial power grid limitations. These challenges underline why access to shared computing infrastructure could be important for countries unable to support large facilities independently. What Challenges Could Affect the Programme?. Although shared computing can reduce the need for individual countries to build expensive data centres, the programme will still depend on adequate electricity, connectivity and supporting infrastructure. Regulatory requirements may also influence how quickly participating countries can adopt the proposed arrangements. The initiative therefore includes assessments of national computing requirements rather than prescribing a single infrastructure model for every market. title: Philippines selected by World Bank for initial rollout of global digital and AI strategy
excerpt: . MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines has been selected by the World Bank for the initial implementation of its Global Digital and Artificial Intelligence (AI) Strategy, aimed at strengthening digital connectivity, technological capabilities, and cybersecurity in the country. According to an announcement dated October 22, 2026, the initiative is expected to support the expansion of affordable internet access, development of digital skills, adoption of artificial intelligence, and improvement of cybersecurity measures nationwide. The partnership aligns with the government’s goal of expanding digital access by 2030, particularly in underserved and geographically isolated communities. Through the initiative, the World Bank is expected to assist the Philippines in strengthening its digital infrastructure and improving access to technologies that can support education, employment, business development, and public services. The strategy also highlights the growing importance of AI in economic development, with efforts focused on equipping Filipinos with digital competencies needed to participate in an increasingly technology-driven economy. Advertisement. Improved cybersecurity is another key component of the initiative, as expanding digital services requires stronger safeguards against online threats and cybercrime. The Philippines’ inclusion in the initial rollout reflects the World Bank’s support for the country’s digital transformation agenda and efforts to promote inclusive technological development. The initiative is expected to contribute to the government’s long-term objective of making digital services more accessible, affordable, and secure for Filipinos by 2030. Advertisement. Share this:. title: Police arrest two suspects in AI-powered bank fraud that cost victims €380,000

Police arrest two suspects in AI-powered bank fraud that cost victims €380,000. Wednesday, 21 October 2026 - 21:10. Rotterdam police arrested two suspects accused of a new form of bank-helpdesk fraud. The operation allegedly caused around €380,000 in losses for 170 victims in just three weeks. The suspects allegedly used AI-generated phone calls and a fake banking app to copy victims' bank cards remotely, allowing accomplices to withdraw thousands of euros. Victims came from across the Netherlands and ranged in age; dozens were in their twenties and thirties. The suspects are a 23-year-old man from Vaassen, in Gelderland, suspected of developing the technology used in the fraud and directing other members of the group, and a 25-year-old man from Ede, also in Gelderland, suspected of coordinating the criminal operation. A Rotterdam court's pretrial detention chamber ruled on Tuesday that both men must remain in custody for at least another 90 days while the investigation continues. Victims received a phone call with a prerecorded message warning of suspicious activity on their bank accounts. The callers used artificial intelligence (AI) to produce dozens of recordings featuring different voices, banks, companies, and scenarios. Victims were asked to press 1 if they did not recognize the alleged activity. They were then connected to someone posing as a bank employee. The supposed bank employee followed a prepared script, pressuring victims to act quickly to block their bank cards. Victims were instructed to download an app and hold their bank cards against their phones to scan them. The criminals presented this as a way to secure the accounts. According to police, the app transmitted data from the card's near-field communication (NFC) chip to an app used by an accomplice. NFC is the technology that enables contactless payments. A person operating the second app was ready at a cash machine or payment terminal. The accomplice could then withdraw thousands of euros without the victim realizing what was happening. Police described this technical method as one they had not encountered before. The investigation began in mid-September, when Dutch banks reported cases of the new fraud method through the Electronic Crimes Task Force (ECTF), a partnership involving banks, police and prosecutors that shares information and expertise to tackle financial and digital crime. Within days of consultations with the task force, Rotterdam's cybercrime team had identified the group's digital infrastructure. Investigators monitored the servers and mapped the operation's structure, including the people responsible for the technology, the phone calls and the cash withdrawals.

title: Künstliche Intelligenz im Bankwesen: Effizienz und Vertrauen müssen Hand in Hand gehen.
excerpt: . Künstliche Intelligenz im Bankwesen: Effizienz und Vertrauen müssen Hand in Hand gehen. Anwendungen künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) bieten Banken einen spürbaren Mehrwert – von Kostensenkungen über Managementunterstützung bis hin zu personalisierten Dienstleistungen. Um diese Ergebnisse weiter auszubauen, müssen Banken geeignete Technologien auswählen, in Datenplattformen investieren und die Risiken während des gesamten Implementierungsprozesses managen. Oktober fand im Rahmen der 7. jährlichen hochrangigen Konferenz und Ausstellung der Bankenbranche (Smart Banking 2026) eine Podiumsdiskussion mit Führungskräften des Bankwesens zum Thema „KI schafft eine neue Generation des Bankwesens: Chancen, Prioritäten und strategische Ausrichtungen“ statt, bei der es darum ging, wie KI in die Praxis integriert werden kann und wie technologische Innovation mit Geschäftseffizienz und Systemsicherheit verknüpft werden kann. In seinen einleitenden Worten wies Dr. Dao Minh Tu, Vizepräsident und Generalsekretär des vietnamesischen Bankenverbandes, darauf hin, dass sich die Bankenbranche von der Digitalisierung von Prozessen und Dienstleistungen hin zur Nutzung von Daten und dem Einsatz von KI wandelt, um Betriebsmodelle neu zu gestalten, Risiken zu managen und das Kundenerlebnis zu verbessern. Laut Tu entwickelt sich KI zu einer Kernkompetenz, die in Entscheidungsprozesse, Arbeitsorganisation und die Schaffung strategischen Mehrwerts für Kreditinstitute integriert wird. Laut Dr. Dao Minh Tu zeigen praktische Erfahrungen bei verschiedenen Geschäftsbanken, dass KI-Anwendungen – je nach Umfang und Implementierungsgrad – dazu beigetragen haben, Kosten zu senken, Mehrwert zu schaffen und Gewinne in Höhe von mehreren zehn bis mehreren hundert Milliarden VND zu generieren. Diese Ergebnisse belegen, dass KI zunehmend den Bereich technologischer Experimente verlässt und direkt zur Geschäftseffizienz und zum Management von Banken beiträgt. Dr. Dao Minh Tu, Vizepräsident und Generalsekretär des vietnamesischen Bankenverbandes, hielt einen Vortrag auf dem Seminar. Die Entwicklung digitaler Bankdienstleistungen bildet die Grundlage für diesen Prozess. Daten aus Transaktionen und Interaktionen im digitalen Umfeld ermöglichen die Analyse von Kundenbedürfnissen, die Personalisierung von Dienstleistungen und einen zeitnahen Kundenservice. Laut den auf dem Seminar präsentierten Informationen erreichten QR-Code-Zahlungen in den ersten acht Monaten des Jahres 2026 über 311 Millionen Transaktionen mit einem Gesamtwert von über 274 Billionen VND. Die Herausforderung besteht jedoch darin, den Übergang von Einzelanwendungen zu einem bankweiten Einsatz zu gestalten, um greifbare Ergebnisse zu erzielen und gleichzeitig die Betriebssicherheit zu gewährleisten und das Kundenvertrauen zu erhalten. Dr. Dao Minh Tu berichtete von seinen Erfahrungen auf seiner Arbeitsreise mit dem australischen Bankenverband, großen Geschäftsbanken und Forschungsinstituten des Landes und erklärte, dass KI für australische Banken von besonderem Interesse sei. Neben der Suche nach Lösungen zur Verbesserung des Managements und der betrieblichen Effizienz konzentrieren sich Finanzinstitute auch auf die Kontrolle der mit der Technologie verbundenen Risiken. Digitale Transformation und KI sind auch zentrale Themen der ASEAN-Bankenkonferenz, die im November auf den Philippinen stattfindet. Laut Dr. Dao Minh Tu müssen Banken angesichts der ständigen Entwicklung neuer KI-Lösungen Technologien identifizieren, die ihren Bedürfnissen, Einsatzbedingungen und dem vietnamesischen Rechtsrahmen entsprechen. The session, to be held on October 23, will explore how artificial intelligence is reshaping financial services and what it means for the legal profession. CITI BANK and MNLU MUMBAI Fireside Chat. Bar & Bench. Published on : 21 Oct 2026, 8:16 am. 2 min read. Copied. Follow Us. Listen to this article. Maharashtra National Law University (MNLU) Mumbai is hosting a Fireside Chat with Citi’s Technology, Operations & Privacy (TOP) Legal team, titled “Artificial Intelligence & the Future of Banking: Opportunities, Risks & Regulatory Frontiers”. The session, to be held on October 23, will explore how artificial intelligence is reshaping financial services and what it means for the legal profession. The event is being organised by the Internship and Placement Cell of the University, in association with the Internal Quality Assurance Cell (IQAC). Artificial intelligence is changing how banks and financial institutions work, from credit assessment, fraud detection and risk management to compliance, customer service and cybersecurity. These changes raise difficult legal questions on data protection, accountability, technology contracting, intellectual property and the pace of regulation. The primary aim of the Fireside Chat is to bring senior in-house counsel from Citi into conversation with the University’s students on these developments. The speakers will discuss how in-house legal teams in a global bank deal with these issues day to day, including how lawyers advise business and technology teams on AI governance, privacy, cybersecurity and procurement and what this means for students aiming for in-house roles in banking and technology. The session will be moderated by Dr Garima Pal , Assistant Professor of Law, MNLU Mumbai. The Fireside Chat will feature three senior members of Citi’s Technology, Operations & Privacy Legal team. 1. Adam Marchuck : Adam Marchuck is Managing Director & General Counsel, Technology, Operations, IP & Privacy, at Citi. He leads the legal team advising Citi’s technology and operations stakeholders on procurement and sourcing, cybersecurity, intellectual property and privacy, and on the bank’s approach to artificial Intelligence. 2. Nicholas Fernandez : Nicholas Fernandez is Director and Head, Asia Clusters, International Technology, Operations & Privacy Legal, at Citi. He joined Citi in 2007 and leads legal support for the bank’s Technology and Operations businesses across Asia Pacific. He has over 25 years of experience in private practice and in-house legal roles. 3. Maneesh Thakur : Maneesh Thakur is Senior Vice President, Technology, Operations & Privacy Legal, at Citi. With nearly two decades of legal experience, he advises on technology, procurement, outsourcing and cross-border commercial transactions across the APAC region. The session will also see participation from other distinguished members of Citi’s legal team, namely Jyoti Tiwarekar , Vineet Bachhawat , Debasrita Saratkar , Saket Prakash , Shraiya Thapliyal , Sakshi Verma and Krashanu Pundir from the Technology, Operations & Privacy Legal team, and Nisha Mistry from the Citi Investor Services Legal team. title: Smart Banking 2026: Die Verbindung von KI-Anwendungen mit Kundenvertrauen.
excerpt: . Smart Banking 2026: Die Verbindung von KI-Anwendungen mit Kundenvertrauen. Die Konferenz Smart Banking 2026 hob die Rolle der KI bei der digitalen Transformation des Bankwesens hervor, die das Kundenvertrauen stärkt und die operative Sicherheit gewährleistet. VietnamPlus • 22/10/2026. Am 22. Oktober 2026 fand in Hanoi die 7. Smart Banking 2026 Konferenz und Ausstellung unter der Schirmherrschaft der vietnamesischen Staatsbank statt, organisiert vom vietnamesischen Bankenverband in Zusammenarbeit mit der IEC Group. Unter dem Motto „Gestaltung einer neuen Ära des Bankwesens auf der Grundlage von KI, Kundenvertrauen und digitaler Resilienz“ brachte die Veranstaltung Vertreter von Aufsichtsbehörden, Führungskräfte im Bankwesen, Finanzinstitute und Technologieunternehmen aus dem In- und Ausland zusammen, um über Wege und Lösungen zur Förderung der digitalen Transformation im Bankwesen zu diskutieren. In seinen Ausführungen betonte der stellvertretende Gouverneur der vietnamesischen Staatsbank, Pham Tien Dung, dass die digitale Transformation des Bankensektors in eine neue Phase eintritt, die den effektiven Einsatz künstlicher Intelligenz (KI), die Aufrechterhaltung des Kundenvertrauens und die Stärkung der Widerstandsfähigkeit gegenüber zunehmend komplexen Risiken erfordert. Das Bankensystem verarbeitet derzeit täglich rund 100 Millionen Zahlungstransaktionen mit einem Gesamtvolumen von etwa 1,2 Billionen VND. Bei einigen Banken werden über 95 % der Transaktionen digital abgewickelt. Diese Größenordnung stellt immer höhere Anforderungen an die Effizienz der Technologieanwendung und die operative Sicherheit. Laut dem stellvertretenden Gouverneur muss KI in erster Linie einen konkreten Mehrwert schaffen. Entscheidend ist, welche Probleme diese Technologie löst, wie sie zu einem besseren Kundenservice beiträgt, wie Banken effizienter arbeiten und wie Risiken frühzeitig erkannt werden können. KI muss in die Gesamtentwicklungsstrategie integriert und mit Daten, Geschäftsprozessen, Personalwesen und Governance-Modellen verknüpft werden. Dies ist die Verantwortung jeder einzelnen Bank, nicht nur der IT-Abteilung. Der stellvertretende Gouverneur forderte die Kreditinstitute auf, die Vorschriften der vietnamesischen Staatsbank zu Sicherheit und Risikomanagement bei KI-Anwendungen eingehend zu prüfen und umzusetzen. Nguyen Hung, Generaldirektor der TPBank, schilderte seinen Weg von der digitalen Transformation zum intelligenten Banking und erklärte, dass die digitale Transformation zwar die Skalierung fördert, die neue Phase jedoch von Banken einen Wandel von der „Digitalisierung von Prozessen“ hin zur „Intelligenzierung des Ökosystems“ erfordere. Dabei werde KI zu einem zentralen Wachstumstreiber, da sie den Kontext verstehe und Kunden proaktiv betreue. Das könnte Sie interessieren. Mit einem Kundenstamm von 18 Millionen und 99,5 % Transaktionen, die über digitale Kanäle abgewickelt werden, sieht die TPBank in der Kombination aus KI, Datenkultur und menschlichen Kontrollfähigkeiten den Schlüssel, um Skaleneffekte in einen echten und nachhaltigen Wettbewerbsvorteil zu verwandeln. Neben der Notwendigkeit einer effektiven KI-Anwendung betonte Vizegouverneur Pham Tien Dung, dass mit zunehmender Digitalisierung Vertrauen zu einem entscheidenden Faktor für das Bankensystem wird. Dieses Vertrauen muss durch die Fähigkeit gestärkt werden, Vermögenswerte, Daten und Kundenrechte bei jeder Transaktion zu schützen. Der gesamte Bankensektor hat seine Bemühungen verstärkt, Daten zu identifizieren, zu verifizieren und zu bereinigen sowie frühzeitig vor risikobehafteten Transaktionen zu warnen. Die vietnamesische Staatsbank hat zudem eine verbesserte Anwendungssicherheit und die Bereitstellung von Tools gefordert, mit denen Kunden ihre Konten proaktiv schützen können, darunter eine Funktion zur Festlegung einer Wartezeit für erstmalige Geldtransfers.
